## Language Understanding

Search engines work best when customers type short, precise keywords — but real shoppers often describe what they want in everyday language. When the search engine can only match exact words in product titles, any customer who phrases their need as a question or a description walks away empty-handed. For a home and kitchen retailer like Imerco, this is a significant revenue risk: customers who know what they want but can't find it don't come back.

**"noget til at opbevare madrester i køleskabet"**
When a customer searched for something to store leftovers in the fridge, the search returned nothing at all — even though the store carries food storage containers, airtight boxes, and fridge organisers in the Madopbevaring og organisering category. The engine saw a descriptive sentence and found no matching product titles, so it gave up entirely instead of connecting the description to the right product type.

**"hvad kan jeg bruge til at lave kaffe om morgenen"**
A customer asking what they could use to make coffee in the morning also received zero results — despite the store stocking coffee makers, French presses, espresso machines, and coffee accessories. The engine treated this as a literal keyword search, found no product titled "hvad kan jeg bruge til at lave kaffe om morgenen," and returned a blank page.

**"noget der kan holde blomster på spisebordet"**
The search returned nothing for a customer describing something to hold flowers on the dining table — a clear intent for a vase or floral centrepiece. The store carries vases and home décor, but none of the words in the query ("noget," "holde," "blomster," "spisebordet") appear literally in any product title, so the engine retrieved nothing rather than inferring the customer meant a vase.

**"jeg skal bage en kage og mangler det rigtige udstyr"**
A customer explaining that they needed to bake a cake and were missing the right equipment saw a completely empty results page, even though the store has an entire Bageudstyr category. The engine could not extract "baking equipment" as the underlying intent from a full conversational sentence, so a customer with a clear purchase need was turned away.

**"kaffekande"**
This query did return relevant results — every product shown was a termokande, which is a direct synonym — but the page was dominated by repeated variants of the same item. Eva Solo Termokande occupied ten of the fifteen result slots, including two entries at 299,95 kr and two at 264,95 kr. The Cook & Baker Termokande, which scored highest of any product on the page, was pushed down behind these repeated cards, and distinct alternatives from Alfi and Aarke were similarly crowded out.

---

## Shopping Context

Customers frequently search by occasion or mood rather than by product name — "wedding gift," "something luxurious," "cosy mugs." When the search engine can only match words that appear in product titles, these high-intent searches either return nothing or return a thin, poorly ordered set. Occasion and seasonal queries are often the highest-value searches on a home goods site, so failures here have a direct impact on revenue.

**"indflytningsgave til nyt hjem"**
When a customer searched for a housewarming gift for a new home, the search returned nothing at all — even though the store carries candles, kitchenware, home décor, and textiles that are exactly the kind of products people buy as housewarming gifts. None of those words appear in product titles, so the engine found no match and showed a blank page.

**"konfirmationsgave til ung pige"**
A search for a confirmation gift for a young girl also returned zero results, despite the store stocking decorative items, candles, textiles, and kitchenware that are standard purchases for this occasion. The engine had no way to connect "konfirmationsgave" to any product category, leaving a customer with clear buying intent at a complete dead end.

**"julegaver til køkkenentusiaster"**
The search returned nothing for a customer looking for Christmas gifts for kitchen enthusiasts — one of the most commercially valuable query types a kitchen retailer can receive. The store's entire kitchen range is relevant here, but because no product is literally titled "julegaver til køkkenentusiaster," the engine retrieved nothing.

**"gave til mor på morsdag"**
This Mother's Day gift query returned only a single product: the Kähler Hammershøi Sommer Vase. While a vase is a plausible gift, the near-empty result set means the store's full range of gift-appropriate items — serving sets, candles, tableware, textiles — was invisible to this customer. The engine appears to have matched on a narrow keyword rather than understanding this as a broad gift-occasion query.

**"sommer udsalg køkkenudstyr"**
A customer searching for summer sale kitchenware saw zero results, even though the store has both an "Udsalg og tilbud" category and a kitchenware range. The engine could not connect a query combining two of its own category names with a seasonal modifier to any actual products.

---

## Filters & Constraints

When a customer adds a colour, material, or brand to their search — "black pots," "white mugs," "red Le Creuset" — they expect every result to match that constraint. If the search engine treats those words as optional hints rather than hard requirements, customers have to manually scan through irrelevant results or give up. Negation queries ("knives not Zwilling," "lamps not floor lamps") are an even more direct signal of intent that the engine must respect.

**"knive ikke Zwilling"**
When a customer explicitly asked for knives that were not Zwilling, the search returned zero results — even though the store carries kitchen knives from multiple other brands. The engine appears to have tried to match the full phrase as a keyword and found nothing, rather than searching for knives and excluding the named brand.

**"kander uden plastik"**
A search for jugs or carafes without plastic also returned nothing, despite the store having a Kander og karafler category. The engine could not parse "uden plastik" as a material exclusion and instead returned a blank page where a full range of glass or stainless steel jugs should have appeared.

A customer searching for black pots was shown 15 results, but the colour constraint was not enforced. Products like the Cook & Baker Stegegryde and Victoria Emaljeret Gryde appeared without any indication they were black, sitting alongside the Eva Trio Black line Gryde which does state its colour. The engine treated "sort" as a keyword hint rather than a filter, so the customer had to judge for themselves which products were actually black.

**"Le Creuset gryde rød"**
All 11 results were Le Creuset pots — the brand and product type were matched correctly — but the colour "rød" (red) was ignored entirely. Every result in the set was a Le Creuset pot in an unspecified colour, meaning a customer who wanted a specific red pot had to scroll through the full range without any guarantee they were seeing red products.

## Product Discovery

Product discovery covers the engine's ability to map the words customers use to the categories and products the store actually sells. When a customer uses a common everyday phrase for a product type, or splits a compound category name into two words, the engine should recognise the intent and return the right category — not a random assortment of loosely related items.

**"potter og pander"**
When a customer searched for pots and pans using this everyday phrase, all three results were art posters: Poster&Frame Vilhelm Lundstrøm Plakat - Opstilling med kander appeared three times in a row. The engine matched the words "potter" and "pander" against a painting title rather than recognising this as a cookware query, so a customer looking for the Gryder og stegepander category was shown wall art instead.

**"sofabord og sidebord"**
A search for a coffee table and side table returned zero results, even though the store carries furniture in its Møbler category. These are standard everyday terms for living room furniture, but the engine found no keyword overlap with any product and returned a blank page rather than directing the customer to the relevant furniture range.

**"badeværelse tilbehør"**
Searching for bathroom accessories as two separate words returned only four results — a Zone Skraber m. Holder, two CASA Living electric toothbrush products, and a toothbrush head — when the store's Badeværelsestilbehør category should contain a much broader range. The engine treated the spaced form as a different query from the compound category name, so most of the bathroom accessories range was invisible.

---

## Brand & Model Search

Brand searches are among the highest-converting queries on any retail site — a customer who types a brand name already knows what they want and is close to buying. The main risk here is not relevance but variety: when multiple size or colour variants of the same product fill the results page, customers see less of the brand's range and the best-scoring distinct products get buried.

**"Kähler vase"**
The Kähler Hammershøi Sommer Vase at 399,95 kr occupied four of the fifteen result slots (positions 1, 3, 4, and 14), and the Kähler Hammershøi Minivasesæt appeared twice at different price points. This left the highest-scoring product on the page — the Kähler Hammershøi Vase at 399,95 kr with a relevance score of 0.898 — buried at position 10, displaced by lower-scored duplicates of other variants. The customer saw a page that felt repetitive rather than one that showcased the breadth of the Kähler vase range.

## Prioritized Roadmap

1. **Handle conversational and natural-language queries by mapping intent to product categories**
Fixes the Language Understanding and Shopping Context capabilities, where queries like "noget til at opbevare madrester i køleskabet," "hvad kan jeg bruge til at lave kaffe om morgenen," "indflytningsgave til nyt hjem," and "julegaver til køkkenentusiaster" all returned zero results because the engine could not connect descriptive or occasion-based phrasing to any product category. Implement a query-understanding layer — whether rule-based intent mapping, semantic/vector search, or an LLM-based query rewriter — that extracts the core product need from conversational input and maps it to the relevant category before the keyword search runs. As an immediate safety net, configure a zero-results handler that detects key intent words ("opbevare," "lave kaffe," "bage," "gave," "morsdag," "konfirmation," "julegaver") and redirects to the appropriate category page rather than showing a blank page.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Major Project

2. **Apply colour, material, and brand constraints as hard filters, not keyword hints**
Fixes the Filters & Constraints capability across queries like "gryder sort," "krus hvid," "Le Creuset gryde rød," "Bodum kaffekande sort," and "Rosendahl skål hvid," where the colour token was treated as an optional keyword rather than a structured filter, allowing off-colour products to appear throughout the result set. Parse recognised colour terms and material descriptors as structured facet filters applied at retrieval time, so only products matching the stated attribute are returned. This same fix should also enforce brand-exact matching to prevent Rosenthal results appearing in a Rosendahl search.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

3. **Implement negation parsing so "ikke" and "uden" act as exclusion filters**
Fixes the Filters & Constraints capability for queries like "knive ikke Zwilling," "kander uden plastik," "lamper ikke gulvlampe," and "vinglas uden stilk," all of which returned zero results because the engine could not parse a negation instruction. Detect "ikke [BrandName]" and "uden [attribute]" patterns, strip the negation phrase from the keyword query, and apply the corresponding exclusion as a filter — brand exclusion for brand negations, attribute exclusion for material or type negations. As an interim fallback, if full negation parsing is not yet feasible, at minimum re-run the search on the core noun alone so the customer sees relevant products rather than a blank page.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

4. **Map colloquial category terms, occasion phrases, and compound/split words to the correct taxonomy**
Fixes the Product Discovery and Shopping Context capabilities, where queries like "potter og pander" returned art posters instead of cookware, "sofabord og sidebord" returned nothing despite a furniture range, "badeværelse tilbehør" (split form) retrieved only four results from a broad category, and seasonal queries like "sommer udsalg køkkenudstyr" found nothing despite matching site categories existing. Build a synonym and intent-mapping dictionary that connects everyday colloquial terms, occasion phrases, and spaced variants of compound category names to the correct internal taxonomy nodes — so the engine routes these queries to the right category before any keyword matching occurs.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

5. **Collapse product variants so each distinct model appears once in results**
Fixes duplicate flooding in Language Understanding (Eva Solo Termokande filling ten slots for "kaffekande"), Brand & Model Search (Kähler Hammershøi Sommer Vase occupying four slots for "Kähler vase"), and Filters & Constraints (Bodum Caffettiera Stempelkande filling eleven of fifteen slots for "Bodum kaffekande sort"). Implement result deduplication keyed on product model and brand so that size, colour, and price variants of the same item are collapsed into a single card — with variants accessible via a selector — freeing up result slots for distinct products and ensuring the highest-scoring item in each model group is the one that surfaces.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Medium Effort

6. **Build occasion-to-category mapping for gift and seasonal queries**
Fixes the Shopping Context capability for high-value queries like "gave til mor på morsdag" (which returned only the Kähler Hammershøi Sommer Vase), "konfirmationsgave til ung pige," and "indflytningsgave til nyt hjem." Create a curated occasion taxonomy — Mother's Day, confirmation, housewarming, Christmas — and tag gift-appropriate products across categories (candles, tableware, textiles, kitchenware, home décor) so that occasion queries retrieve a broad, commercially relevant assortment rather than a single product or nothing at all. Seasonal landing pages tied to search redirects provide an immediate merchandising fallback while the broader tagging work is completed.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

7. **Recognise subjective qualifiers as ranking signals, not required keywords**
Fixes Shopping Context failures for "luksuriøst køkkengrej," "hyggelige krus og kopper," and "elegant borddækning," where the presence of a qualitative modifier caused zero or near-zero results because the engine required the word to appear literally in a product title. A maintained list of common qualitative terms that should never block retrieval will prevent this entire class of failure.

roadmap_narrative:
1. **Handle conversational and natural-language queries by mapping intent to product categories**
Fixes the Language Understanding and Shopping Context capabilities, where queries like "noget til at opbevare madrester i køleskabet," "hvad kan jeg bruge til at lave kaffe om morgenen," "indflytningsgave til nyt hjem," and "julegaver til køkkenentusiaster" all returned zero results because the engine could not connect descriptive or occasion-based phrasing to any product category. Implement a query-understanding layer — whether rule-based intent mapping, semantic/vector search, or an LLM-based query rewriter — that extracts the core product need from conversational input and maps it to the relevant category before the keyword search runs. As an immediate safety net, configure a zero-results handler that detects key intent words ("opbevare," "lave kaffe," "bage," "gave," "morsdag," "konfirmation," "julegaver") and redirects to the appropriate category page rather than showing a blank page.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Major Project

2. **Apply colour, material, and brand constraints as hard filters, not keyword hints**
Fixes the Filters & Constraints capability across queries like "gryder sort," "krus hvid," "Le Creuset gryde rød," "Bodum kaffekande sort," and "Rosendahl skål hvid," where the colour token was treated as an optional keyword rather than a structured filter, allowing off-colour products to appear throughout the result set. Parse recognised colour terms and material descriptors as structured facet filters applied at retrieval time, so only products matching the stated attribute are returned. This same fix should also enforce brand-exact matching to prevent Rosenthal results appearing in a Rosendahl search.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

3. **Implement negation parsing so "ikke" and "uden" act as exclusion filters**
Fixes the Filters & Constraints capability for queries like "knive ikke Zwilling," "kander uden plastik," "lamper ikke gulvlampe," and "vinglas uden stilk," all of which returned zero results because the engine could not parse a negation instruction. Detect "ikke [BrandName]" and "uden [attribute]" patterns, strip the negation phrase from the keyword query, and apply the corresponding exclusion as a filter — brand exclusion for brand negations, attribute exclusion for material or type negations. As an interim fallback, if full negation parsing is not yet feasible, at minimum re-run the search on the core noun alone so the customer sees relevant products rather than a blank page.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

4. **Map colloquial category terms, occasion phrases, and compound/split words to the correct taxonomy**
Fixes the Product Discovery and Shopping Context capabilities, where queries like "potter og pander" returned art posters instead of cookware, "sofabord og sidebord" returned nothing despite a furniture range, "badeværelse tilbehør" (split form) retrieved only four results from a broad category, and seasonal queries like "sommer udsalg køkkenudstyr" found nothing despite matching site categories existing. Build a synonym and intent-mapping dictionary that connects everyday colloquial terms, occasion phrases, and spaced variants of compound category names to the correct internal taxonomy nodes — so the engine routes these queries to the right category before any keyword matching occurs.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

5. **Collapse product variants so each distinct model appears once in results**
Fixes duplicate flooding in Language Understanding (Eva Solo Termokande filling ten slots for "kaffekande"), Brand & Model Search (Kähler Hammershøi Sommer Vase occupying four slots for "Kähler vase"), and Filters & Constraints (Bodum Caffettiera Stempelkande filling eleven of fifteen slots for "Bodum kaffekande sort"). Implement result deduplication keyed on product model and brand so that size, colour, and price variants of the same item are collapsed into a single card — with variants accessible via a selector — freeing up result slots for distinct products and ensuring the highest-scoring item in each model group is the one that surfaces.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Medium Effort

6. **Build occasion-to-category mapping for gift and seasonal queries**
Fixes the Shopping Context capability for high-value queries like "gave til mor på morsdag" (which returned only the Kähler Hammershøi Sommer Vase), "konfirmationsgave til ung pige," and "indflytningsgave til nyt hjem." Create a curated occasion taxonomy — Mother's Day, confirmation, housewarming, Christmas — and tag gift-appropriate products across categories (candles, tableware, textiles, kitchenware, home décor) so that occasion queries retrieve a broad, commercially relevant assortment rather than a single product or nothing at all. Seasonal landing pages tied to search redirects provide an immediate merchandising fallback while the broader tagging work is completed.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

7. **Recognise subjective qualifiers as ranking signals, not required keywords**
Fixes Shopping Context failures for "luksuriøst køkkengrej," "hyggelige krus og kopper," and "elegant borddækning," where the presence of a qualitative modifier caused zero or near-zero results because the engine required the word to appear literally in a product title. Treat terms like "luksuriøst," "hyggelige," and "elegant" as soft boosting signals — use them to surface higher-priced, premium-brand, or editorially tagged products — while driving retrieval from the core product noun alone ("køkkengrej," "krus og kopper," "borddækning"). A maintained list of common qualitative terms that should never block retrieval will prevent this entire class of failure.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win
